system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2129-04-06 13:14:00 to 2129-04-08 14:25:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, bipolar disorder, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for recurrent severe abdominal pain following a fatty meal and a viral illness. He reported episodes of passing out attributed to pain, which were evaluated and determined to be likely pseudoseizures. Imaging showed no acute intracranial or thoracic abnormalities. He was managed with IV fluids, pain control, anti-nausea medication, and gradual advancement to a low-fat diet. His symptoms improved, he tolerated oral intake, and he was discharged home with a short supply of pain medication, stool softeners, and instructions to follow up with his primary care provider and gastroenterologist.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

diagnoses.long_title: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I was in the shower and the pain got so bad I just passed out. My wife called EMS. It’s my stomach again—sharp pain in the middle, going to my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of chronic pancreatitis. Did something trigger the pain this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a big meal with fried food two days ago. I know I shouldn’t, but I just couldn’t resist. The pain started soon after and just kept getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Fatty meals can definitely flare up pancreatitis. You also mentioned passing out—has that happened before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, every time the pain gets really bad. But only then. I’ve never passed out when I wasn’t in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your records. Neurology looked into this before and found no seizure activity on EEG. They think these episodes are related to pain—what we call psychogenic nonepileptic events.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a real seizure? But it feels like I black out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a real experience, but it’s not caused by abnormal brain activity. Severe pain can cause your body to shut down briefly—like a vasovagal response. The CT of your head was normal, so no bleeding or stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. I was worried something was really wrong up there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a CT of your abdomen. It shows changes from chronic pancreatitis—pancreatic atrophy and calcifications—but no new blockages or acute issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just another flare-up? I’ve had so many of these.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely triggered by the fatty meal. We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your pancreas rest. You’ll get fluids and pain meds through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I have to stay like this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a day or two, until your pain improves and we can start you on a clear diet. We’ll advance it slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m back to check on you. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but better since the IV meds. I’m really worried about the weight loss though—I’ve lost about 40 pounds in three weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s significant. It’s likely from not eating well due to pain and nausea. We’ll work on getting your nutrition back on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also had a high blood sugar at home—470. I have diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. Your glucose was 158 when you arrived. We’re monitoring it and will use a sliding scale insulin to keep it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to end up in trouble with that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your lab results. Your white blood cell count is a bit high—13.9—which suggests inflammation, not infection. Your lipase is normal, which supports this being a chronic flare, not acute pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the acidosis they mentioned in triage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a mild anion gap acidosis. Your lactate was normal, but you had ketones in your urine. This points to starvation ketosis—your body is burning fat for fuel because you haven’t been eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s because I’m not eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve started you on IV fluids with dextrose—D5NS—to correct that. It should resolve in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your pain is better, and you’ve had no nausea. We’re going to start you on a clear liquid diet and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I have broth or juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, things like that. We’ll advance to a full liquid diet, then low-fat solids if you do well. No fatty foods—those are a trigger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on the clear diet. We’re switching your pain meds from IV to oral. You’ll get oxycodone 15 mg twice a day with 5 mg for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that stronger than what I was taking at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a structured plan to manage your pain safely. We’re also keeping your other meds—like duloxetine, lisinopril, and simvastatin—on schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking—what can I do long-term? I keep coming back with this pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great question. We consulted your gastroenterologist, Dr. Patel. She’ll see you soon to discuss options like a celiac plexus block or surgery if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t seen her in a while. I guess I’ve been avoiding it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But regular follow-up is key. She’ll help you get ahead of these flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re eating regular food, pain is controlled, and your labs have improved. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What should I do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on a low-fat diet, take your meds as prescribed—including omeprazole and prochlorperazine for nausea—and avoid alcohol completely. Follow up with your PCP and Dr. Patel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the oxycodone as directed. If it’s not controlled or you can’t keep fluids down, come back. But try to avoid triggers—especially fatty foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thanks for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Any nausea or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel much better. Still some ache, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll send you home with a short supply of pain meds and instructions. Your wife can help you stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Remember—low-fat diet, meds, and follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll do my best this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just wanted to say thanks again before I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay healthy.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, bipolar disorder, and alcohol abuse in remission was admitted after passing out in the shower due to severe epigastric pain following a fatty meal. Imaging showed no acute intracranial or abdominal process, with findings consistent with chronic pancreatitis. His pain was managed with IV fluids, bowel rest, and IV analgesics, transitioning to oral oxycodone. An anion gap acidosis was identified and attributed to starvation ketosis, which resolved with dextrose-containing IV fluids. His syncope was deemed consistent with psychogenic nonepileptic events triggered by pain. He tolerated a gradual diet advancement, pain improved, and he was discharged home with medication adjustments, dietary instructions, and follow-up plans with his primary care provider and gastroenterologist.
